title: On experience and reflection in teaching
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino opens with a case study of a novice teacher, Mr K, who observes an experienced colleague's lesson, faithfully replicates the same explanation-then-questioning structure, and still ends up with a disengaged class -- prompting the question of why identical technique produces different results. She argues the difference is not raw years of experience but reflection in disguise, and illustrates how self-reflection can go wrong with an example of a teacher who tries mini-whiteboards, finds the routine slow to build, and concludes the tool isn't worth the time -- a conclusion Castelino calls flawed if the actual goal (raising participation and thinking ratio) was never achieved by another route either. She argues that reading and observation are valuable but often insufficient, and that what actually helped Mr K was a further step: discussing the specific in-the-moment decisions behind the experienced teacher's lesson -- how she decided what to include, when to pause and question, and how she read cues that the class was struggling. Castelino closes with a personal admission that when a trainee once asked her to explain her own in-the-moment decisions, her honest answer was "I just knew what to do" -- an unhelpful response in the moment that nonetheless prompted her to examine and later explain her own reasoning, which she argues is the discussion process most likely to transfer real expertise between teachers.
points: Castelino's Mr K case study shows that copying an experienced teacher's visible structure is not sufficient -- the same technique, executed identically, produced a disengaged class because the underlying in-the-moment decisions weren't transferred.

She flags a specific way self-reflection goes wrong: a teacher abandoning mini-whiteboards because the routine felt slow to build, without checking whether the goal those whiteboards served (higher participation and thinking ratio) was achieved a different way.

Her proposed fix beyond reading and observation is structured discussion with the observed teacher about specific decisions: what to include in an explanation, when to pause for questions, how to read cues of struggle.

Castelino's personal admission -- that her own honest answer to a trainee's question was once \"I just knew what to do\" -- shows even experienced teachers need to be pushed to articulate tacit decision-making before it can transfer to someone else.
quotes: Mr K wants to improve his practice and asks to observe a more experienced teacher, Ms Y.
It could be due to Ms Y’s experience. The mistake I used to make is to equate experience with time spent teaching. But experience is way more than that: it is reflection in disguise.

This teacher might reflect on this and think using mini-whiteboards is not worth the effort and time it is taking to build a routine of whole class participation and thinking. But if the purpose of using the mini-whiteboards (increasing ratio) is not achieved via another, possibly more effective strategy in this context, then the self-reflection is flawed.
Reading something in a book and then observing it in action is incredibly useful CPD. However, in Mr K’s case, it wasn’t enough.
Simply knowing about the importance of techniques such as Checking for Understanding is not enough to help teachers improve their practice.

I have been Ms Y (possibly not as successful as her!) where a trainee once asked me similar questions and I replied with ‘I just knew what to do’. Entirely unhelpful, I know, but it did make me go away and think about how I responded to the class and the decisions I made.
